title: At the doctor's
goal: Explain what hurts, understand the doctor's advice, and master two things at once: the *mă doare* pattern — the aching part is the subject, you are on the receiving end — and the imperative, the form for commands.
bekal: say what hurts with *mă doare* (one thing) and *mă dor* (several), without "I have"
describe how your body feels with the dative: *mi-e rău, mi-e foame, mi-e sete, mi-e somn, mi-e frică*
understand and give commands: *luați!* for someone you address formally, *ia!* and *nu lua!* for a friend

dialogs.title: Dialogue — La cabinetul medical

notes: **Mă doare capul — not "capul meu doare".** This is the heart of the unit. The verb *a durea* means "to hurt (someone)": the aching part (*capul*) is the **subject**, and you are the one affected, in the accusative form *mă*. Literally "the head hurts me". Since the owner is already clear from *mă*, the body part just takes the definite article — no *meu*. The pattern is the same as *îmi place* in unit 10: the thing talked about is the subject, and you just feel the effect.

**Mă dor picioarele.** Since the body part is the subject, the verb agrees with **the body part**, not with the person: one → *doare*, several → *dor*. *Mă doare un picior* (one leg), *mă dor picioarele* (both). Exactly like *place* versus *plac*.

**Luați, deschideți, spuneți, beți, stați** — all the doctor's commands are polite imperatives, and they are identical to the *voi* form of the present tense. You've been using them since unit 6 without noticing: *Scuzați-mă*, *Mergeți drept înainte*, *Traversați*. Nothing new to learn.

**Stai, bea, nu ieși.** Andrei uses *tu*, so his commands are short: *stai!* (stay), *bea!* (drink). The negative has an odd but easy rule: **nu + infinitive** — *nu ieși!*, *nu lua!*, *nu bea!*. So "don't drink" isn't *nu bei* but *nu bea*.

**De trei ori pe zi** = three times a day. The pattern: *o dată* (once), *de două ori* (twice), *de trei ori*, then *pe zi / pe săptămână / pe lună*. And *domnule doctor* is the form of address (vocative) of *domnul* — doctors in Romania are always addressed this way, or *doamna doctor* for a woman doctor.

grammars.title: Mă doare versus mă dor — the aching part is the subject
body: English says "my head hurts"; Romanian says "the head hurts me". The person in pain appears as an **accusative** pronoun from unit 12 (*mă, te, îl, o, ne, vă, îi, le*), and the body part takes the definite article.
The verb has only two forms to remember: **doare** for one body part, **dor** for more than one.
after: **If the person is named**, the doubling from unit 12 applies: *Pe Andrei îl doare un dinte.* *Pe Ioana o doare capul.* The short pronoun must still be there.
**In the past** the pattern follows unit 15: *M-a durut capul toată ziua* (my head hurt all day), *m-au durut picioarele*. The negative is regular: *Nu mă doare nimic* — "nothing hurts".

**Body states use the dative, not the accusative.** The *mi-e cald / mi-e frig* pattern from unit 16 works for every feeling: *mi-e rău* (I feel sick), *mi-e foame* (hungry), *mi-e sete* (thirsty), *mi-e somn* (sleepy), *mi-e frică* (scared). For others just swap the pronoun: *ți-e foame?*, *îi este somn*, *ne e sete*, *vă e frig?*. Don't say *sunt foame* — in Romanian hunger is "to you", not "what you are".

grammars.title: The imperative — telling and forbidding
body: The imperative has only two kinds of listener: **tu** (one person, informal) and **voi / dumneavoastră** (several people, or one person addressed formally). The second form is free — the same as the present tense. The *tu* form needs a little attention.

head: Infinitive
tu
voi / dumneavoastră
Negative for tu
rows: a sta — to stay, to stay still

after: **A guide for the *tu* form:** most verbs use the *el/ea* present form — *așteaptă!*, *ascultă!*, *spune!*, *deschide!*, *citește!*. Some others use the *tu* present form, especially verbs with no object: *mergi!*, *dormi!*, *stai!*, *vezi!*. A few short ones are irregular and very common: **fă!**, **zi!** (say), **vino!**, **fii!** (be — *Fii atent!* "be careful!").

**Negative:** for *tu* use **nu + infinitive without *a*** — *nu lua!*, *nu face!*, *nu fi trist!*. For *voi / dumneavoastră* just put *nu* before the normal form: *nu luați!*, *nu beți cafea!*, *nu mergeți la lucru!*.

**Short pronouns move after** the command and are hyphenated: *Scuzați-mă!*, *Așteaptă-mă!* (wait for me), *Ia-o!* (take it), *Spune-mi!* (tell me). In the negative they come back in front: *Nu mă aștepta!*. Reflexive verbs behave the same: *Trezește-te!* (wake up!), *Nu te culca târziu!*
To keep a command from sounding rude, add *te rog* or *vă rog* — or use *Poți să…? / Puteți să…?* from unit 11.

blocks.text: After *mă doare* and *mă dor* body parts always take the definite article, so get your ear used to these forms: *capul, gâtul, stomacul, piciorul, spatele* · *gura, mâna, burta, inima* · *ochii, dinții, genunchii* · *urechile, mâinile, picioarele, degetele*. Note *mână → mâini*: the plural is irregular, and since hands usually come in pairs, it's the plural you'll hear most. *Spate* doesn't change in the plural, while *ochi* and *genunchi* are the same in singular and plural — the difference shows only in the article: *ochiul* (the eye, one) versus *ochii* (both eyes).

blocks.title: The kissed hand: Sărut mâna
items: ***Sărut mâna*** literally means "I kiss the hand" — a respectful greeting used by men to women, and by younger people to older women. Nobody actually kisses the hand anymore; only the phrase remains.
Budi uses it with Mrs. Popescu every morning. It isn't used with older men; *Bună ziua* is enough.
Children also say it as "thank you" to a grandmother or aunt after a meal. The usual reply: *Să crești mare!* — "may you grow up big!"

head: Sentence
English
rows: I don't feel well. · I feel sick.
Do you have anything for a cough?

blocks.text: Good news for English speakers: half the Romanian medical vocabulary looks familiar — *doctor, farmacie, sirop, pastilă, antibiotic, alergic, gripă, temperatură, vitamină*. It's the everyday words that need practice: *răceală* comes from *rece* (cold), just like the English "a cold". *Îmi curge nasul* is literally "the nose runs to me" — a possessive dative that comes at the next level; for now learn it whole.

blocks.title: Getting sick in Romania: what to know
items: **112** is the single emergency number — ambulance, police, fire department. Pharmacies are marked with a green cross, and antibiotics are only given with a *rețetă*.
**Sănătate!** or **Noroc!** is what you say when someone sneezes — Romania's "bless you". *Multă sănătate!* is a common wish when leaving a sick person — and on birthdays, too.

**Curentul** — the cross-breeze from two open windows — is blamed by many Romanians for colds, earaches, and stiff necks. You'll hear *Te trage curentul!* ("you'll catch a draft!") from Mrs. Popescu the moment a window and a door are open at the same time.
The first home remedy offered is almost always tea: *ceai de tei* (linden blossom) or *ceai de mușețel* (chamomile), with honey and lemon.
